title: Beginner French
summary: Start speaking French: greetings and introductions, tu and vous, pronunciation and numbers, nouns, gender and articles, être, avoir and present-tense verbs, questions and negation, and everyday phrases for family, food, shopping and time.
audience: Complete beginners, students, travellers and professionals working with French-speaking countries

body.p: French is spoken by hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is an official language in many African countries, including Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar and Rwanda. It is useful for travel, trade, diplomacy and study.

list: Bonjour: hello, good morning (used during the day).
Bonsoir: good evening.
Salut: hi, bye (informal, with friends).
Comment ça va ? / Ça va ?: How are you?
Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ? / Et vous ?: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Je m'appelle Amina: My name is Amina.
Comment tu t'appelles ? (informal) / Comment vous appelez-vous ? (formal): What is your name?
Enchanté(e): pleased to meet you.
Au revoir: goodbye. À bientôt: see you soon.
S'il vous plaît / s'il te plaît: please. Merci: thank you. De rien: you're welcome.

body.p: French has two words for "you". Use tu with friends, family, children and peers; use vous with strangers, elders, officials and anyone you should show respect to, and always for more than one person. When unsure, use vous.

body.tip: Practise a short self-introduction aloud every day: "Bonjour, je m'appelle…, j'habite à…" (I live in…).

list: Final consonants are often silent: "petit" sounds like "puh-tee".
The French "r" is made at the back of the throat.
Nasal vowels, as in "bon", "vin" and "un", are pronounced through the nose.
"u" (as in "tu") is said with rounded lips while saying "ee".
Liaison: a silent final consonant is often pronounced before a vowel: "vous avez" sounds like "voo-za-vay".

body.p: 1 un, 2 deux, 3 trois, 4 quatre, 5 cinq, 6 six, 7 sept, 8 huit, 9 neuf, 10 dix, 11 onze, 12 douze, 13 treize, 14 quatorze, 15 quinze, 16 seize, 17 dix-sept, 18 dix-huit, 19 dix-neuf, 20 vingt, 30 trente, 40 quarante, 50 cinquante, 60 soixante, 100 cent.

In standard French, 70 is soixante-dix (sixty-ten), 80 is quatre-vingts (four twenties) and 90 is quatre-vingt-dix (four twenties and ten). Belgian and Swiss French often use septante (70) and nonante (90).

body.tip: Count objects around you in French, and say prices aloud when shopping.

body.p: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the article changes accordingly. Learn each noun with its article.

list: Definite (the): le (masculine), la (feminine), l' (before a vowel or silent h), les (plural): le livre (the book), la maison (the house), l'école (the school), les enfants (the children).
Indefinite (a, some): un (masculine), une (feminine), des (plural): un stylo (a pen), une table (a table), des amis (some friends).
Plurals usually add -s, which is normally silent: le livre, les livres.

body.p: Adjectives agree with the noun and usually come after it: une voiture rouge (a red car), des voitures rouges. Many add -e for feminine: un petit garçon, une petite fille. A few common adjectives come before the noun: beau, bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux.

body.tip: Write new nouns in two colours, one for masculine and one for feminine; visual memory helps with gender.

body.p: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Example: Je suis étudiant(e) (I am a student). Elle est sénégalaise (She is Senegalese).
j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. Example: J'ai deux frères (I have two brothers). Avoir is also used for age: J'ai vingt ans (I am twenty years old).

Most verbs end in -er. Remove -er and add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Parler (to speak): je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent. The -e, -es and -ent endings sound the same. Other common -er verbs: habiter (to live), travailler (to work), aimer (to like), manger (to eat; nous mangeons).

body.tip: Learn être and avoir by heart first; they are the most used verbs and help form other tenses later.

list: Rising intonation: Tu parles français ? (You speak French?)
Est-ce que: Est-ce que tu parles français ?
Question words: Qui ? (who), Quoi ? / Qu'est-ce que ? (what), Où ? (where), Quand ? (when), Pourquoi ? (why), Comment ? (how), Combien ? (how much, how many).
Examples: Où habites-tu ? / Où est-ce que tu habites ? (Where do you live?) Combien ça coûte ? (How much does it cost?)

body.p: Put ne before the verb and pas after it: Je parle anglais → Je ne parle pas anglais (I don't speak English). Ne becomes n' before a vowel: Je n'ai pas de voiture (I don't have a car); note that un, une and des become de after a negative. In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: Je sais pas (I don't know).

body.tip: Learn "Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?" (Can you repeat, please?) and "Je ne comprends pas" (I don't understand); they keep conversations going.

lessons.title: Everyday French: family, food and shopping

body.p: la mère (mother), le père (father), le frère (brother), la sœur (sister), les parents (parents), l'enfant (child), le grand-père, la grand-mère. Possessives agree with the noun: mon père, ma mère, mes parents.

list: Je voudrais… : I would like… (polite)
un café, du thé, de l'eau, du pain, du riz, du poulet, des fruits (coffee, tea, water, bread, rice, chicken, fruit)
Combien ça coûte ? / C'est combien ? : How much is it?
L'addition, s'il vous plaît : The bill, please.
J'ai faim / J'ai soif : I'm hungry / I'm thirsty (using avoir).

body.p: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche (Monday to Sunday; not capitalised). Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?) Il est trois heures (It is three o'clock). French often uses the 24-hour clock: 15 h 30 is 3:30 p.m.

body.tip: Label items in your home with sticky notes in French; you will see the words dozens of times a day.

quiz.q: How do you say "good evening" in French?
Which form of "you" should you use with an elder you have just met?
